src: site, modelled on FA24 Exam 2, Q1D
model:
[[mech:grignard-co2-cyclohexyl]]

Four arrows in all. The Grignard reagent behaves as R:⁻ and attacks the carbon of {{CO2}}. The acid is a separate, second step.

rubric.h: First arrow: from the C-Mg bond to the carbon of {{CO2}} (Grignard as nucleophile, the carbon of {{CO2}} as electrophile)
Second arrow: one C=O pi bond onto its oxygen
The carboxylate intermediate, with O⁻ and ⁺MgBr
Workup: O⁻ lone pair to an H of {{H3O+}}, and the H-O bond onto the oxygen of water
The neutral carboxylic acid as the product

steps.h: The C-Mg bond is polarized toward carbon. Treat cyclohexylmagnesium bromide as a cyclohexyl carbanion, R:⁻, with ⁺MgBr next to it.

ask.q: Which atom of the Grignard reagent carries the electrons that will react?

steps.h: {{CO2}} has no hydrogen at all, so there is no proton to take. The reagent must act as a nucleophile. In O=C=O the carbon is electron poor: two oxygens pull electrons away from it.

ask.a: The carbon. The oxygens are electron rich.

steps.h: Arrow from the C-Mg bond to the carbon of {{CO2}}. That carbon would then have five bonds, so the electrons of one C=O pi bond move onto that oxygen. Two arrows.
A carboxylate: the ring carbon is bonded to C(=O)O⁻, with ⁺MgBr as the counter-ion.
{{H3O+}} is added afterwards. A lone pair on O⁻ takes a proton, and the H-O electrons stay on water. Two arrows. The product is cyclohexanecarboxylic acid.

ask.q: Why can the acid not be added at the start?
ask.a: It would protonate R:⁻ to give cyclohexane, and no C-C bond would form.

solution.answer: Step 1: the C-Mg electrons attack the carbon of CO2 and a pi bond opens onto oxygen (carboxylate). Step 2: H3O+ protonates the carboxylate. Product: cyclohexanecarboxylic acid.
solution.rule: R:⁻ attacks the electron-poor carbon. Acid comes last.

steps.h: Isopropylmagnesium bromide is R:⁻ with ⁺MgBr. The electrons are in the C-Mg bond, on the middle carbon.

ask.q: Is R:⁻ a strong or a weak base?
ask.a: Very strong. Its conjugate acid, an alkane, has {{pKa}} 50 to 60.

steps.h: {{D2O}} is water with D in place of H. It has an acidic O-D ({{pKa}} about 15.7), so this is an acid-base reaction.

ask.q: Which way does the equilibrium lie?
ask.a: Far to the right: the stronger acid ({{D2O}}, 15.7) gives its D to the stronger base and the weaker acid (the alkane, 50 to 60) forms.

steps.h: First arrow: from the C-Mg bond to a D of {{D2O}}. Second arrow: from that D-O bond onto oxygen.
Propane with a D on the middle carbon, and {{DO-}} with ⁺MgBr.

ask.q: On which carbon is the D?
ask.a: On the carbon that was bonded to magnesium.

solution.answer: Two arrows: C-Mg bond to D, D-O bond to O. Products: 2-deuteriopropane and DO⁻ ⁺MgBr.
solution.rule: R-MgX + D2O gives R-D, with D where the metal was.

src: site, modelled on FA24 Exam 2, Q1D
stem:
A student wants butanoic acid and adds {{CO2}} and {{H3O+}} to the Grignard reagent at the same time. What is the main organic product?
[[rxn:CCC[Mg]Br>CO2, H3O+;together>"?"]]

choices.why: R:⁻ is a very strong base and {{H3O+}} is a strong acid. The proton transfer happens at once and gives propane, before any carbon-carbon bond can form.
This needs two separate steps: {{CO2}} first, acid afterwards. With acid present from the start, the reagent is destroyed.
The carbon of a Grignard reagent is the electron-rich atom. It takes a proton. It is not attacked by water's oxygen.
The reagent does not go back to the alkyl bromide. Acid gives R-H.

steps.h: Propylmagnesium bromide is {{CH3CH2CH2:-}} with ⁺MgBr.

ask.q: What does a very strong base do when an acid is in the flask?
ask.a: It takes a proton, faster than anything else it could do.

steps.h: {{H3O+}} has {{pKa}} −1.5 and the alkane 50 to 60. Protonation of the carbanion is enormously favourable and very fast. {{CO2}} never gets its turn.

ask.q: What does "1) {{CO2}}; 2) {{H3O+}}" tell you to do?
ask.a: Add {{CO2}} first, let it react completely, and only then add the acid.

steps.h: R:⁻ + {{H+}} gives R-H: propane.
The acid is the last step, written as step 2. Its job is only to put the proton on the carboxylate.

solution.rule: Acid destroys a Grignard reagent: R:⁻ + H⁺ gives R-H. Acid comes last.

stem:
What is the organic product?
[[rxn:CC[Li] + O>>"?"]]

choices.why: Ethyllithium is {{CH3CH2:-}}, a very strong base. It takes a proton from water ({{pKa}} 15.7) and becomes ethane. The other product is LiOH.
This treats the carbon as electron poor, as it is in an alkyl halide. In C-Li the carbon is the electron-rich end.
Nothing here removes a hydrogen from the next carbon. The reagent is the base, and it gains a hydrogen.
Two ethyl groups do not join. The carbanion finds the acidic hydrogen of water first.

steps.h: C-Li is polarized {{d-}} on carbon: {{CH3CH2:-}} {{Li+}}.
Water, {{pKa}} 15.7. The conjugate acid of the carbanion is ethane, {{pKa}} 50 to 60.
The C-Li electrons take an H of water, and the H-O electrons stay on oxygen: ethane and {{Li+}} {{-OH}}.

stem:
Which conditions turn 1-bromobutane into a Grignard reagent?
[[rxn:CCCCBr>?>CCCC[Mg]Br]]

choices.why: The lecture's recipe: R-X + Mg in diethyl ether gives R-MgX.
This is the recipe for the organolithium reagent, butyllithium, with LiBr as the other product. It contains no magnesium.
Water would protonate the reagent as fast as it formed. The product would be butane.
The magnesium has to be the metal, Mg, which gives up its electrons to the C-Br bond. {{Mg^2+}} has none to give.

steps.h: Grignard: R-X + Mg, diethyl ether. Organolithium: R-X + 2 Li, pentane.
The solvent must have no acidic hydrogen. Ether and pentane qualify. Water and alcohols do not.
It is the metal itself that reacts, written Mg or {{Mg^0}}.

solution.rule: R-X + Mg in ether gives R-MgX. R-X + 2 Li in pentane gives R-Li.

stem:
Draw the curved arrows.
[[rxn:CC[Mg]Br + CCO>>CC + CC[O-]]]

steps.h: Ethylmagnesium bromide is {{CH3CH2:-}} with ⁺MgBr.
Ethanol's O-H, {{pKa}} about 16. The C-H hydrogens of ethanol are not acidic.
From the C-Mg bond to the H of the O-H. From the H-O bond onto oxygen. Products: ethane and ethoxide with ⁺MgBr.

solution.answer: Two arrows: C-Mg bond to H, H-O bond to O. Products: ethane and CH3CH2O⁻ ⁺MgBr.
solution.rule: Any O-H protonates a Grignard reagent.

src: site, modelled on FA24 Exam 2, Q1D
stem:
Methylmagnesium bromide reacts with {{CO2}}. What has formed after this first step, before any acid is added?
[[rxn:C[Mg]Br + O=C=O>>"?"]]

choices.why: The methyl carbon bonds to the carbon of {{CO2}}, and one pi bond opens onto oxygen. The result is a carboxylate (acetate), with ⁺MgBr beside it.
Here the methyl carbon has bonded to an oxygen. The oxygens of {{CO2}} are electron rich. The electron-poor atom is the carbon.
Acetic acid needs a proton, and there is no proton source until the acid is added in the second step.
Methane would need an acidic hydrogen. {{CO2}} has no hydrogen.

steps.h: {{CO2}} has no hydrogen, so the reagent cannot act as a base. It acts as a nucleophile.
The carbon of O=C=O, pulled on by two oxygens.
C-Mg bond to the carbon of {{CO2}}, and one C=O pi bond onto oxygen. The product is acetate, still an anion.

solution.rule: R:⁻ attacks the carbon of CO2. The product stays an anion until acid is added.

stem:
Draw the curved arrows.
[[rxn:CCCC[Li] + CC#C>>CCCC + CC#[C-].[Li+]]]

steps.h: Butyllithium is a butyl carbanion with {{Li+}}.
Propyne has two kinds of hydrogen. The one on the triple-bond carbon ({{sp}}) has {{pKa}} 25. The {{CH3}} hydrogens are {{sp3}} C-H, {{pKa}} 50 to 60.
25 is far below 50 to 60, so the alkyne hydrogen is transferred to the butyl carbon.
From the C-Li bond to the alkyne H. From that C-H bond onto the alkyne carbon, as a lone pair.

solution.answer: Two arrows: C-Li bond to H, C-H bond onto the alkyne carbon. Products: butane and lithium propynide.
solution.rule: A terminal alkyne (pKa 25) is acidic enough to protonate R:⁻.

stem:
Draw the mechanism and all the products.
[[rxn:[Li]c1ccccc1 + [2H]O[2H]>>"?"]]
model:
Phenyllithium is a carbanion, R:⁻ {{Li+}}, and {{D2O}} is the acid. Two arrows: from the C-Li bond to a D, and from that D-O bond onto oxygen.

[[rxn:[Li]c1ccccc1 + [2H]O[2H]>>[2H]c1ccccc1 + [Li+].[O-][2H]]]

The D is on the ring carbon that carried the lithium. The other product is LiOD.

rubric.h: First arrow starts at the C-Li bond and ends at a D of {{D2O}}
Second arrow: the D-O bond onto oxygen
Benzene with one D, on the carbon that carried Li
{{Li+}} and {{DO-}} shown as the other product

steps.h: The ring carbon bonded to Li is the electron-rich atom.
{{D2O}} has an acidic O-D, just as water has an acidic O-H.
C-Li bond to D, D-O bond to O. The carbon gains D exactly where Li was.

solution.answer: Deuteriobenzene and LiOD, by one proton-transfer step with two arrows

stem: Which of these liquids can be the solvent for a Grignard reagent without destroying it?

choices.why: Diethyl ether has only C-H hydrogens ({{pKa}} 50 to 60). It has no proton the reagent can take, and it is the solvent the lecture uses.
Methanol has an O-H, {{pKa}} about 15.5. The reagent takes that proton and becomes R-H.
Water, {{pKa}} 15.7, protonates the reagent at once.
The hydrogen on the triple-bond carbon has {{pKa}} 25, still far below 50. The reagent takes it and becomes R-H.

steps.t: Recall how basic the reagent is
steps.h: R:⁻, conjugate acid {{pKa}} 50 to 60.
O-H in methanol and water. The alkyne C-H in 1-hexyne. None in diethyl ether.
15.5, 15.7 and 25 are all far below 50: each of those liquids destroys the reagent.

solution.rule: The solvent for R-MgX or R-Li must have no acidic hydrogen.

stem:
A student wants the labelled alcohol shown as the product and tries this route. What goes wrong?
[[rxn:OCCCCBr>1) Mg, ether;2) D2O>[2H]CCCCO]]

choices.h: Nothing: the route gives the product shown
choices.why: The starting bromide carries its own acid, the O-H. The C-Mg carbon never survives to meet {{D2O}}.

choices.h: As soon as a C-Mg bond forms, that carbon takes the O-H hydrogen of a neighbouring molecule, so the carbon ends up with H and not D
choices.why: An alcohol O-H has {{pKa}} about 16, far below 50 to 60. The carbanion is protonated to a {{CH3}} group, and the {{D2O}} added later can only put D on the oxygen.

choices.h: Magnesium cannot react with a primary C-Br bond
choices.why: Primary bromides make Grignard reagents without trouble. The problem is the OH group.

choices.h: Ether is the wrong solvent: an alcohol should be used so that everything dissolves
choices.why: An alcohol as solvent would destroy any Grignard reagent, for the same reason the OH group in this molecule does.

steps.t: Look at the whole starting material
steps.h: It has a C-Br bond, which is what Mg needs, and also an O-H.
The moment a carbanion-like carbon forms, it is surrounded by O-H groups of other molecules. {{pKa}} 16 against 50 to 60: the proton transfer is fast and complete.
The carbon gets H from the O-H, so the chain ends in an ordinary {{CH3}}. The oxygen is left as an alkoxide, and {{D2O}} in step 2 gives O-D, not C-D.

solution.answer: The reagent destroys itself: the C-Mg carbon is protonated by the O-H, so no D ends up on carbon.
solution.rule: A molecule with an O-H or N-H cannot be turned into a Grignard reagent.

stem:
Propyne is treated with ethylmagnesium bromide, then with {{CO2}}, then with {{H3O+}}. The product is {{C4H4O2}}. Draw the mechanism of each step.
[[rxn:CC#C>1) CH3CH2MgBr;2) CO2, then H3O+>CC#CC(=O)O]]
model:
Step 1, proton transfer. The Grignard reagent is a base. Arrow from the C-Mg bond of ethyl to the H on the triple-bond carbon ({{pKa}} 25), and arrow from that C-H bond onto the alkyne carbon. Ethane ({{pKa}} 50 to 60) leaves, and the alkyne carbon now carries the negative charge, with ⁺MgBr.

[[rxn:CC[Mg]Br + CC#C>>CC + CC#C[Mg]Br]]

Step 2, attack on {{CO2}}. The new carbanion is a nucleophile. Arrow from the alkyne carbon's pair (its C-Mg bond) to the carbon of {{CO2}}, and arrow from one C=O pi bond onto oxygen: a carboxylate.

[[rxn:CC#C[Mg]Br + O=C=O>>CC#CC(=O)[O-]]]

Step 3, workup. Arrow from an O⁻ lone pair to an H of {{H3O+}}, and arrow from the H-O bond onto water's oxygen.

[[rxn:CC#CC(=O)[O-] + [OH3+]>>CC#CC(=O)O + O]]

rubric.h: Step 1: two arrows of the proton transfer, taking the hydrogen on the triple-bond carbon (not a {{CH3}} hydrogen)
Ethane and the alkynyl anion (with ⁺MgBr) as the products of step 1, with {{pKa}} 25 against 50 to 60 as the reason
Step 2: the alkyne carbon attacks the carbon of {{CO2}}, and a pi bond opens onto oxygen
The carboxylate intermediate with its charge
Step 3: protonation by {{H3O+}} (two arrows) and the neutral acid, {{C4H4O2}}

steps.t: Take the reagents one at a time
steps.h: First ask what ethylmagnesium bromide does to propyne. Propyne has an acidic hydrogen ({{pKa}} 25), so the Grignard reagent acts as a base.
Ethane, and a new carbanion on the alkyne carbon. It is a weaker base than the ethyl carbanion, but it is still R:⁻.

steps.t: Give the new R:⁻ its partner
steps.h: {{CO2}} has no hydrogen, so the alkyne carbanion attacks its carbon, exactly as in the exam question.
The carboxylate takes a proton from {{H3O+}}.
But-2-ynoic acid: four carbons, four hydrogens, two oxygens. One carbon more than propyne, from {{CO2}}.

solution.answer: Proton transfer (ethane leaves), then attack of the alkynyl carbanion on the carbon of CO2, then protonation: but-2-ynoic acid.
solution.rule: Acidic hydrogen present: the reagent is a base. None: it is a nucleophile. Ask again at every step.

src: site, modelled on FA24 Exam 2, Q1D
stem:
A student's mechanism for this reaction has three mistakes, listed below. Correct each one and say why it is wrong. [[rxn:Br[Mg]c1ccccc1>1) CO2;2) H3O+>OC(=O)c1ccccc1]]
  1. The first arrow starts at the Mg atom and points to the ring carbon.
  2. The ring carbon is shown making its new bond to an oxygen of {{CO2}}.
  3. {{H3O+}} is drawn in the same step as {{CO2}}.
model:
1. The arrow must start at the C-Mg bond and point away from the ring, to the atom being attacked. An arrow shows where electrons go, and the electrons are in that bond (the reagent is R:⁻ ⁺MgBr).
  2. The new bond goes to the carbon of {{CO2}}. That carbon is electron poor because two oxygens pull on it. The oxygens are electron rich. A second arrow moves one C=O pi bond onto oxygen.
  3. The acid is a separate second step. If {{H3O+}} were present with the Grignard reagent it would protonate R:⁻ and give benzene. It is added afterwards to protonate the carboxylate.
[[mech:grignard-co2-benzoic-acid]]

rubric.h: Mistake 1: the arrow starts at the C-Mg bond, with the reason (that is where the electrons are)
Mistake 2: attack on the carbon of {{CO2}}, with the reason (electron poor), and the pi electrons moved to oxygen
Mistake 3: acid only in the second step, with the reason (it would destroy the reagent: R-H)

steps.h: A curved arrow starts at an electron pair. Magnesium is the electron-poor end of the C-Mg bond, so no arrow starts there.
The carbanion-like carbon looks for the electron-poor atom of {{CO2}}, which is its carbon.
Step numbers on an arrow mean separate additions. A strong acid and a carbanion cannot be in the flask together.

solution.answer: Start the arrow at the C-Mg bond; attack the carbon of CO2 and open a pi bond onto oxygen; add the acid only afterwards.
solution.rule: Arrow from the C-metal bond, to the electron-poor carbon, acid last.
